is essential and has significant practical implications for inducing desired behaviors and mitigating diseases.
Recent breakthroughs using network controllability revealed how individual brain regions can affect the whole brain, guided by the brain's structural framework.
Yet, controlling entire brain activity might be impractical, and it is not always necessary.
A more crucial inquiry is whether individual brain areas can regulate specific target subsystems, although this area of research remains poorly understood.
Furthermore, as people age, the brain's network undergoes continuous changes, yet little is known about its effects on controllability properties.
To investigate these questions, we developed a new approach to quantify the centrality of brain nodes in regulating specific target brain systems.
We then analyzed target control centrality in brain networks of healthy individuals from ages five to 85.
Our key findings show that the sensorimotor system possesses significant control capacity, yet it is difficult for other brain areas to influence it.
We also found that target control centrality changes with age and that the temporal-parietal regions, critical in target control, demonstrate significant decline with aging.
Interestingly, aging affects target control centrality differently depending on the specific brain system considered, and these results contradict previous studies.
Ultimately, by understanding the age-related changes in target control centrality, we may be able to develop more effective strategies for inducing desired behaviors and, potentially, treat neurological disorders.

Despite agreement on a universal neuronal process across species, understanding the dynamics of social media information is significantly lacking. Various laws and processes exist to describe social media propagation but their application is not consistent. By analyzing nearly one billion time-stamped social media events over ten years, our study demonstrates that information propagation on online platforms is both a universal and critical process. Our findings provide foundational understanding for developing future theories and uncover underlying mechanisms driving social media information propagation. CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a new dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test our model's robustness, we conducted repeat studies on the same patients with different annotations. Our model produced a high overall Dice score of 0.82, indicating good tumor segmentation, and consistently outperformed other popular network architectures including Unet, Resnet, and Attentionnet. We observed a significant boost in performance with the use of attention mechanisms and found that proximal tumors were consistently identified despite air pockets and feeding tubes

To accomplish this, our study enhances the field of view for deep neural networks using two core components from the visual processing systems of vertebrates, known as on-center and off-center pathways. This pathway system consists of excitatory centers and inhibitory surrounds, and we refer to it as OOCS for simplicity. The on-center pathway responds positively to the presence of light within its core area but not in its periphery, while the off-center pathway responds positively to the absence of light within its core area but not in its periphery. Our OOCS pathways are developed using a difference of Gaussians, with the variance calculated analytically based on the size of the receptive fields. This pathway system effectively complements each other's responses to light stimuli, enabling a robust edge-detection ability, and ultimately leads to more accurate and reliable inferences in challenging lighting environments. Our experimental findings demonstrate that networks using the OOCS edge representation outperform standard deep models in terms of accuracy and illumination-resistance. Furthermore, our approach successfully replicates these results in the context of color imagery. Notably, our findings also show that networks using the OOCS edge representation tend to generalize better than conventional deep models, and this effect is most pronounced under conditions of low lighting. This research showcases the potential for insights from vertebrate visual processing systems to enhance the performance of deep neural networks. , substantial datasets are crucial - having a vast amount of data allows researchers and engineers to create dependable AI algorithms. For medical imaging tasks, transferring this information from originating healthcare institutions to development organizations poses time-consuming obstacles, including adherence to regulations such as HIPAA and GDPR. There is also the threat of confidential patient data exposure. A potential solution to these challenges is utilizing the Federated Learning framework. Federated Learning enables the development of robust AI models by incorporating diverse data sources, allowing them to generate better outcomes without moving all the data to a central location. Our research employed the FL framework for training a deep learning model in addressing a binary classification problem of detecting COVID-19 presence. By combining three distinct data sources, training separate models, and then training an overarching model with the data, we observed an enhancement in accuracy. The results revealed that the FL model exhibited improved predictive capabilities, displaying higher overall accuracy, better AUC-ROC values, and enhanced specificity and sensitivity compared to using a single dataset. These findings indicate that the Federated Learning framework can effectively train AI models on diverse medical imaging datasets while safeguarding patient confidentiality. As such, this framework offers a promising solution for training robust and accurate neural networks in a secure environment. Our research demonstrates the feasibility of FL for handling disparate datasets, which could be particularly beneficial when working with pandemic data or other sensitive health datasets. In the future, we intend to expand our research by training more complex models and including additional data sources from a variety of healthcare institutions.

iman's seminal paper from 1927, which has been widely cited and is considered a foundational work in the study of algebraic curves. Wiman presents a solution to a problem posed by Ferdinand von Lindemann, confirming the finiteness of the number of algebraic curves of a particular degree that pass through a given set of points in a projective space. Notably, Wiman's proof relies on the assumption that a particular hypothesis, known as the finiteness conjecture, holds true. This hypothesis states that a single polynomial with complex coefficients cannot be identically zero for an infinite number of complex points. Building on Wiman's work, other notable mathematicians have further developed and refined his results, with a notable example being Giulio Codazzi in 1839 and Federigo Enriques in 1893. This translated paper aims to make Wiman's influential work more accessible to a new generation of mathematicians.

addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are commonly used to mitigate sparsity by transferring knowledge from a source domain to a target domain. However, these methods have limitations: single-target CDR applies unnecessary knowledge transfer, increasing noise, and dual-target CDR only addresses knowledge transfer but fails to consider the knowledge reception at the target domain. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework, HRCR, an holistic cross-domain recommender that simultaneously enables knowledge transfer and reception between domains. In the source domain, HRCR derives item representations from both user and item perspectives, and then transfers the knowledge to the target domain by integrating the representations. Moreover, to ensure the target domain's unique characteristics are respected, we add a domain-specific regularization to the knowledge transfer. To further enhance the target domain's representation, we introduces a reception module that receives the transferred knowledge and blends it with the target domain's unique characteristics. Through extensive experiments on two real-world datasets, HRCR is proven to be an superior cross-domain recommender, outperforming current state-of-the-art models. accord with Lin et al.'s observation that the best methods for partial

Between typical outbursts separated by approximately 270 days, a shorter, less intense outburst occurs about 29 days prior to the main event. This unusual double-peaked pattern is a newly discovered phenomenon in binary systems driven by tidal disruption. We investigated the wide binaries to see if the way their distances change could tell us anything, specifically the way their distances change and their speed, or velocity. an iterative method is employed to solve a linear equation system, speeding up convergence often involves developing optimal preconditioners for the linear solver. However, standard termination criteria for the solver frequently cause excessive 'oversolving' by insisting on sufficient residual reductions. This paper presents an alternative approach to interior point methods that utilizes an inner termination criterion not dependent on the residual. It also includes indicators to facilitate suitable transfer to the outer iteration. This inner criterion significantly reduces computation time in each iteration by avoiding unnecessary oversolving. To enable seamless transition to the next IPM iteration, the algorithm ensures sufficient convergence is confirmed before switching. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method leads to substantial performance improvements, particularly in terms of decreased iteration counts and computational costs, as evident from numerical examples. Moreover, the concept of inner termination criteria may be applied to other numerical methods beyond IPMs. Consequently, this approach enhances the efficiency of convergence for such methods. Additionally, adopting this concept enables these methods to achieve natural breaks between computation-intensive steps, thereby facilitating a smoother workflow. It is established that one of the chief advantages of inner termination criteria is the capability to directly utilize the discrete linear system derived from the problem of interest, eliminating the need for an intermediate continuous solution. This capability is a key characteristic distinguishing discrete direct methods from indirect methods. Consequently, this paper aims to contribute to the ongoing research aimed at integrating discrete direct methods into numerical optimization problems. Several concrete proposals are presented in this study to further enhance the performance of discrete direct methods. These proposals

The emergence of memristive properties in transition metal oxides is generally attributed to the electromigration of oxygen vacancies at a nanoscale.  Focusing on Pt/TiOx/TaOy/Pt devices, our research investigates the transfer of oxygen vacancies between the device and its environment in response to electrical stress.  Through both experiments and theoretical simulations, we establish that the TiOx and TaOy layers undergo oxidation during the electroforming process due to the absorption of environmental oxygen.  Once the memristive effect stabilizes, our results indicate that the exchange of oxygen with the environment is minimized and the driving force behind the memristive behavior is restricted to internal electromigration within the TiOx and TaOy layers.  The findings presented here provide essential insights for designing stable and reliable memristive devices composed of binary oxide layers.  The discussion of the environmental influence on oxygen vacancy dynamics also contributes to the broader understanding of the fundamental principles governing binary oxide memristors. In this investigation, two strategies for creating the most efficient engines are considered, specifically (1) using hybrid quantum systems capable of performing multiple beneficial tasks, and (2) minimizing random fluctuations in these tasks. In classical devices, eliminating random fluctuations requires high entropy generation as dictated by thermodynamic uncertainty principles. This theorem pairs a topological module with the module consisting of its continuous homomorphisms to the quotient of the field over the ring. For a certain subset of these modules, the double application of this duality yields a perfect pairing, demonstrating a natural homeomorphism. Furthermore, a natural topology can be constructed on any module, making its double dual map injective and continuous. This allows the module's topological properties to be fully encoded in algebraic terms, essentially allowing a reevaluation of topological considerations in a purely algebraic context. Interestingly, this framework doesn't restrict consideration to any particular ring; instead, any module of interest can serve as the ground field. Consequently, the usual duality between a ring and its quotient field takes on a pivotal role. This equivalence can now be seen as an instance of a more general theorem, illustrating the deep algebraic underpinnings of topological number theory. Ultimately, the module in question can be shown to be representable as a certain type of module over a p-adic ring, yielding a possible demonstration of Borel's theorem that avoids reliance on function fields. 
This work has further implications, allowing a reevaluation of the fundamental categories of topological algebra

Most contextual augmentations used for language model pre-training to date have been independent of their surrounding context.
A groundbreaking method called ELECTRA uses a separate generator and discriminator network for context-specific data enhancement, achieving state-of-the-art performance in its applications.

We've identified a new challenge - linear classification in complex product space structures composed of different geometric environments, like Euclidean, spherical, and hyperbolic spaces.
To tackle this problem, we first establish a framework for defining linear classification models within curved, high-dimensional environments that generalize traditional vector-based classification.
Next, we demonstrate that, regardless of the geometry of the space, linear classification models become essentially equivalent to traditional vector-based classification in a flat, high-dimensional space extension.
Consequently, the expressive capabilities of linear classifiers are limited by the intrinsic characteristics of the underlying geometric space, preventing them from capturing distinct features in complex environments, like the spherical and hyperbolic, that are separable due to their non-flat nature.
Our findings highlight the potential for significant performance gains by using curved, high-dimensional classifiers over traditional flat-based classifiers in relevant data sets. Additionally, we provide a method for evaluating the performance of linear classifiers in complex environments. Our research is further validated by developing an efficient testing framework, employing approximate point pair signatures, which enables us to identify distinct features in curved, high-dimensional spaces that are inaccessible to linear classifiers. Our findings are substantiated by experimental results in spherical and hyperbolic environments. 
Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/tgiraud/PPS.

The Canopus protocol efficiently manages large-scale distributed consensus without the need for a single leader, achieving this through a virtual tree structure that limits network traffic and hardware redundancies within the network. The existing Canopus protocol excels at performance, however, struggles when dealing with failures that don't directly affect performance, leading to the development of RCanopus. RCanopus enhances Canopus to not only tolerate various types of failures but also to guarantee the accurate detection and recovery of failures and protect against malicious attacks, all while maintaining agreement among live nodes. The virtual tree structure in RCanopus is built around a virtual tree algorithm that limits network traffic and ensures network integrity, using a two-phase commit mechanism to manage transactions and protect against failures. The result is a failure-tolerant distributed consensus protocol that guarantees accurate failure detection, recovery, and protection from malicious attacks, with the option to agree among live nodes. A detailed analysis shows that RCanopus is capable of detecting failures within three rounds, recovering from failures within six rounds, and recovering from all types of failures in twelve rounds. Through testing using multiple failure types, as well as stress testing with over 500 nodes, the results demonstrate that RCanopus accurately detects and recovers from failures, protecting the distributed consensus against malicious attacks and maintaining agreement among live nodes. We applied an SEIR complex network dynamics model to simulate and assess the vulnerability of these networks. Our results indicated that a significant proportion of email accounts have experienced security breaches, while more than 90% of network nodes exhibit susceptibility to cyber threats. Our research can facilitate the enhancement of email account security for research institutions, while also opening avenues for further exploration in the realm of communication security. Due to confidentiality considerations, we cannot disclose the source from which we acquired the communication network data, as this would reveal sensitive information. Our results are presented anonymously to avoid identifying the institutions in question. Our methodology and findings are presented in accordance with relevant ethical guidelines. Due to the novel nature of our research, we hope that sharing our approach will enable replication and promotion of cybersecurity within research institutions. Our research contributes to the growing body of literature on email account security and cyber threats, while also inspiring further research in the realm of communication security. Our approach can be adapted for analyzing communication networks within other contexts, potentially leading to the development of more secure systems. Our research promotes the importance of proactively addressing potential security breaches in email accounts. Our methodology and results are available

While these techniques bypass the need for feature engineering, the construction of a source code model greatly influences performance in these tasks. Many recent studies have centered on enriching AST-based source code models with contextual dependencies extracted from control flow graphs, yet few have prioritized the representation of basic code segments which form the basis of contextual dependencies. A fundamental concept in addressing these challenges is the mesh, a composite of basic elements where hexahedral units offer enhanced computational advantages. However, mesh integrity relies on the quality of its components. The issue arises when elements take on shapes hindering precise calculations, rendering them unusable. To deliver accurate outcomes, it is crucial to correct such elements' morphology, rendering them valid. This study synthesizes the outcomes of two studies to develop a mesh assessment and correction framework. By combining their findings, we establish a functioning algorithm but also recognize its potential for enhancement, thus introducing multiple improvements to accelerate its processing speed and robustness. The resulting algorithm is subsequently compared with alternative methods through testing. This research presents a new efficient and reliable method to repair flawed meshes, facilitating optimal results. This repair technique shows promising potential in several fields, such as mesh generated by 3D image reconstruction, where the mesh serves as a input for simulation tasks. An example of such application is the simulation of tissue growth, where the mesh is used to calculate tissue expansion. Due to the nature of this growth, the mesh may become corrupted with elements of poor quality. The proposed algorithm can effectively repair such meshes, enabling accurate predictions. Another area of application is the simulation of fluid dynamics in realistic environments. The mesh, a result of reconstruction, may contain errors causing simulation instability. The proposed algorithm can correct such meshes, resulting in stable and accurate simulations. Additionally

The scarcity of relevant data and domain-specific vocabularies complicate this process even further. Recent breakthroughs in pre-trained models like BERT have revolutionized language modeling by leveraging large-scale general text, thereby enhancing their performance. However, these models still struggle with interpreting intent and slot words within specific contexts. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel framework that employs a dual-learning strategy, involving a contextualized model that simultaneously identifies user intent and slot words. The former is recognized through its relation to a set of predefined categories, while the latter is extracted from relevant phrases within the context. To facilitate intent prediction, a binary classification model is trained using contextualized word embeddings, which are then combined with traditional word embeddings in the case of slot prediction. Virtual multi-staining can be achieved by employing various stains on successive tissue sections or by re-coloring a single section. While both methods necessitate tissue section alignment, the task becomes more complex when dealing with sections that have distinct pathological characteristics and are cut to different thicknesses. To address this challenge, we developed an innovative approach for aligning sections with simple, yet robust, techniques. Our method involves generating a common mask from multiple sections by applying an iterative, mutually corrective process, which enables accurate alignment within a few iterations. Our experiments, involving 1512 images with distinct cellular arrangements, demonstrated that our approach yields excellent results, particularly when compared to other established methods. Our findings reveal that section alignment has a notable impact on virtual-microscopy performance, and our approach outperforms other methods in terms of nuclear alignment, cell alignment, and overall image similarity. Our source code and data are publicly available for the benefit of the histology community. As a result of our work, we have successfully achieved high-quality, two-dimensional tissue alignments, paving the way for accurate three-dimensional tissue reconstruction. Our research has far-reaching implications for tasks such as image segmentation, feature extraction, and classification. Although established methods like bisimulation minimization can take advantage of these patterns, they operate directly on the raw state-level structure of the Markov model, ignoring the higher-level semantics defined by the program. A new approach, presented here, targets more efficient state-reduction methods tailored to these specific patterns within the context of the program, resulting in improved performance in practical applications. Bisimulation minimization based on the Monte Carlo method has already shown promise in a probabilistic model checker, but applying it to the structured Markov models yields suboptimal outcomes. A better solution involves using a hierarchical bisimulation minimization algorithm that accounts for the high-level patterns in the program. However, this method is itself computationally intensive. A novel hybrid approach, introduced between these two extremes, allows for more efficient state-reduction on the structured Markov models, preserving the desired high-level semantics. When applied to the structured models resulting from this hybrid, the traditional Monte Carlo-based bisimulation minimization yields improved results, surpassing the previous best outcomes in practical scenarios. A comprehensive case study demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed hybrid approach. Furthermore, combining the hybrid with other techniques yields minimal models that are better suited to probabilistic verification techniques. By comparing CO and dust emission patterns, it appears the CO emission from the rings is not simply a result of disk CO that's been frozen into the ice. The locations in the disk where CO sublimation occurs could serve as key sites for the formation of complex molecules and the origin of volatile material in the solar nebula. It's hypothesized the CO sublimation phenomenon may be more common than initially thought, urging a deeper examination of other protoplanetary rings for evidence of UV photon-truncated structures. momentum distribution of electron-positron pairs was analyzed using the quantum kinetic equation, focusing on the distinct characteristics of Gaussian and Sauter pulse envelopes. Despite the similarity of these pulse shapes, which led to the misconception that they yield interchangeable temporal profiles, a significant difference in the longitudinal momentum spectra of the created pairs was observed in all time regimes. 

For few-cycle oscillations, the pulse envelope imprints itself on the momentum spectrum, particularly evident in the interference pattern that emerges at later times. The Sauter pulse exhibits oscillation onset and amplitude differences compared to the Gaussian pulse, which are intensified by the carrier-envelope phase and frequency chirping. 

Moreover, the absence of notable interference effects for pulses with fewer than five oscillations revealed that the longitudinal momentum spectrum's peak value differs significantly between the two pulse types at both early and late times. However, when considering probabilities, this challenge is even more complicated: research has demonstrated that under the constraint of differential privacy, there are data sources for which the best-case EO comes at a cost of total accuracy loss - meaning an EO-compliant model can only match a simple classifier in terms of accuracy. Our research expands upon this by eliminating the privacy constraint and revealing that certain data sources have a trivial model as the most accurate option when striving for EO. 

We further investigate the trade-offs between achieving fairness (through EO) and model accuracy loss and provide criteria that dictate when fairness and high model accuracy are compatible for a specific data source.

We discovered that achieving EO results in total fair-denial loss - meaning all individuals who would have been approved under a different (fairer) classification system. 

Our research indicates that achieving EO with differential privacy is impossible, and we provide a data transformation technique that allows for accurate and fair decisions under EO when there are no confidential issues involved.

The primary objective is to reduce costs by adjusting machine speeds and devising a streamlined production planning schedule within a predefined timeframe. To reduce data storage demands and overcome limitations in computational power, a new class of efficient lossy data compressors has been utilized in workflow processes, enabling the storage of detailed post-analysis data. In this research paper, we introduce an innovative adaptive approach that dynamically configures lossy data compression for various simulation components using sophisticated quality assessment algorithms. This contribution is multi-faceted: Firstly, we develop a novel method to identify optimal error limits for each simulation partition, demonstrating the feasibility of individualized lossy compression configuration. Secondly, we establish predictive models to estimate the overall data loss caused by lossy compression and calculate compression ratios based on specific partition properties. Thirdly, we create a streamlined optimization strategy to identify the optimal combination of error limits that maximize compression ratios while minimizing post-analysis data loss. Fourthly, our method introduces negligible computational overhead, enabling efficient in situ lossy data compression during simulations. Experimental results confirm the high accuracy and reliability of our models. Furthermore, our adaptive approach achieves up to a 73% improvement in compression ratio for the tested datasets, resulting in minimal data loss while incurring only a 1% increase in computational overhead. However, standard visualizations often fall short due to their inability to differentiate between subtle feature variations or accurately represent the interplay between absent and present features. This issue could be addressed by using more advanced symbolic surrogate models but, since these typically demand symbolic inputs not commonly available in computer vision, we instead explore a new method for extracting a straightforward, easily interpretable binary explanation. This explanation focuses on the most influential regions within a network's response to an input, enabling feature importance to be naturally represented through the output of the main convolutional layers. Our method generates a composite explanation by combining element-wise max-pooling and global averaging to uncover hidden feature interactions and prioritize essential components. This approach yields superior quality and simplicity over existing max-pooling-based methods and demonstrates significant improvement in fidelity in comparison to global averaging methods. multimedia content on social media platforms is putting immense pressure on mobile backhaul networks, making it necessary to find an efficient solution to alleviate this burden. Caching content at network edge in a proactive manner, while considering the interconnectedness of social networks, appears as a viable option to mitigate this problem. Current caching methods rely on thorough knowledge of social networks and mainly focus on direct interactions among individuals, while neglecting the common pattern of content sharing within close social circles. Our proposal is Bingo, a content caching scheme that capitalizes on online social networks' interest-based group structures. Bingo allows mobile network operators to selectively implement it across their network architecture, such as base stations and data centers, by utilizing available data on user behavior and revenue generation. Bingo's key components are Group Identification and Content Selection. Its Group Identification module identifies users' group affiliations based on shared content, while its Content Selection module determines the most frequently accessed and revenue-generating content for each group. Our performance evaluation, conducted using real datasets from Twitter and Facebook, demonstrates that Bingo outperforms existing caching methods by achieving higher average hit probability and revenue, while reducing the overhead associated with placement decisions. Our findings show that Bingo's hit probability and revenue increase exponentially with the size of the group, while the overhead required to optimize placement decreases as the group size grows. Our research also explores two novel optimization techniques, Standard Form Optimization and Complement Form Optimization, allowing Bingo to achieve optimal results in less time by converting sub-optimal placements into standard

Notable examples include zero-shot and few-shot learning methods that rely on either no or a limited number of training samples, reducing the requirement for novel categories. A dedicated head for the novel category is then trained using pseudo-labels derived from the weakly labelled data. A notable advantage of our framework is its ability to discard incorrect pseudo-labels, ensuring that the model only relies on reliable annotations. Moreover, to enhance model generalisation to novel categories, we suggest an approach that reduces the disparity between the distribution of annotated and non-annotated classes by transferring knowledge from related classes with adequate annotations. u-Goldstone (NG) theorem has been undertaken with an emphasis on its underlying mathematical structures drawn from Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory. The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In analyzing this phenomenon, a novel approach reveals that the anomalous NG theorem reflects a synergy between two distinct algebraic operations: the differentiation operator acting on semi-invariant elements and the Lie derivative operator acting on invariant elements. This perspective, rooted in the fundamental properties of Lie algebras, can be applied to both local and global contexts. Notably, our study shows that the anomalous NG theorem may be derived from the general product rule of differential forms. Recent advancements in local Lie algebras enable the resolution of an longstanding issue regarding the application of the anomalous NG theorem to chiral symmetry in the quark-gluon plasma. Moreover, our work uncovers a deep connection between the anomalous NG theorem and the skew-spiral Armario-Carneiro theorem. This research examines profit-sharing agreements between a single Content Provider and multiple Internet Service Providers, with the Content Provider agreeing to split profits in exchange for enhanced service quality. To model these negotiations, we use a Stackelberg game, where the Content Provider decides the distribution of its profits and the Internet Service Providers determine their level of investment effort, while in another scenario, we look into how Content Providers and Internet Service Providers collaborate, with the latter deciding on how much to invest and the former deciding on how to split the profits, in a bargaining game. The results show that when Content Providers and Internet Service Providers collaborate, the equilibrium outcome is reached when the profits are equally distributed. Conversely, in a situation where the Content Provider sets the profit allocation, the Internet Service Providers receive a higher share of the profits. Furthermore, we explore the effect of the number of Content Providers on these equilibrium outcomes. Our findings suggest that increased competition among Content Providers decreases the share of the profits allocated to the collaborating Internet Service Providers and increases the share allocated to the cooperating internet service providers when the content providers set the profit allocation. Conversely, competition among Content Providers has no effect on the share of the profits allocated to the collaborating internet service providers in the collaborative scenario. This research contributes to a better understanding of the dynamic nature of profit-sharing agreements between Content Providers and Internet Service Providers. The findings provide valuable insights for these industry players on how to effectively negotiate these agreements

However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label.  A novel technique known as single-sample adaptation is introduced, which enables the development of Conditional GANs that are capable of learning from such sparse and isolated data. By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that's just a tiny fraction of its potential.  However, at higher accretion rates, absorption from the abundant low-energy photons hinders the gamma-rays, thwarting the MAD model's explanation. A text retrieval engine was developed for an extensive archaeological text collection of around 658 million words. Given the crucial role of domain-specific entities like locations, time periods, and artefacts in archaeological research, a named entity recognition model was developed to annotate the full collection with relevant entities. This paper introduces ArcheoBERTje, a BERT-based model pre-trained on Dutch archaeological texts, to improve named entity recognition in this field. A comparative study was conducted between ArcheoBERTje and generic multilingual and Dutch models, exploring ensemble methods and integrating domain thesaurus using Conditional Random Fields (CRF) for enhanced performance. A thorough analysis of the BERT models was performed, providing valuable insights on the effect of domain-specific pre-training on model performance and its potential to make external knowledge from thesaurus unnecessary. outside of computing, the tension between precision and efficiency is consistently a point of consideration when faced with uncertainty. Since computer science also encounters precision-efficiency trade-offs, the consequences of balancing these competing priorities in the governance of computer systems are relatively underexplored. By referencing established risk assessment protocols in the United States, we argue that similar attention to these trade-offs in the context of distributed machine learning systems is required. These high-stakes and safety-critical systems are particularly pressing as they are comprised of technologies such as self-driving vehicles. To that end, we undertake three key objectives. Firstly, we outline how this trade-off manifests in the context of distributed machine learning systems. Secondly, we point out gaps in current U.S. risk assessment standards that could be filled in order to effectively assess these systems. Lastly, we suggest specific actions to be taken to ensure that accountability measures are put into place for hypothetical accuracy-efficiency risks, in the event that such scenarios materialize as accidents. By promoting these mechanisms, we may ultimately foster a more just, more transparent governance framework, in keeping with public values. Ultimately, we may come to view accountability as a means to rectify injustices in the governance of technology, in particular. Our investigation into this topic is undertaken in light of the relative absence of attention to distributive justice, particularly in the context of distributed machine learning systems. By focusing on high-stakes systems, we may create a pathway for the promotion of justice, in particular distributive justice.

Introduction:
Artificial Intelligence-generated art has gained significant attention in recent years. The primary methods employed for this task are based on Variational Auto-Encoders and Generative Adversarial Networks. The latter has two main variants - Conditional and Unconditional GANs. The Conditional approach conditions the Generator on additional information, typically related to the target distribution, whereas the Unconditional variant conditions the Discriminator. 

Neural Painters are models of the Unconditional variant, utilizing a Generator that produces individual brushstrokes and a Discriminator aiming to differentiate between real and fake brushstrokes. Brushstroke generation is often conditioned on a target distribution in both training and inference processes. 

Our study utilizes Transfer Learning to accelerate Neural Painter training. The main goal of this study is to investigate the feasibility of applying TL to overcome the difficulties and slow training times often associated with GAN-based models.

the processes behind the quenching of low-mass galaxies.  A particularly effective way to explore this is by comparing quenched galaxies within isolated environments to those affected by external processes.  A notable example of external influence comes from group or cluster edges where the quenching of low-mass galaxies can be observed. By studying a galaxy residing at the shell's edge, we can compare its star formation status to that of galaxies within the core, thus gaining insight into external influence on its quenching. The ultimate balance between thermal flux and velocity was previously proposed for this highly driven thermal flow.
Despite ongoing experimental and numerical investigations, direct observation of this critical regime remains unattained so far.
We now demonstrate that the ultimate state of this highly driven thermal flow is achievable once the heat diffusion layer becomes completely isolated from the flow resistance.

While current research into data poisoning attacks focuses on targeted techniques for specific models, it is generally limited to binary classifiers and gradient-based algorithms. To overcome these limitations, a novel label-flipping attack has been developed which doesn't require prior knowledge of the model it's attacking and targets groups of similar data, while constrained by a set budget for altering labels. For this purpose, acoustic testing techniques have been developed that can assess the material's state of elastic deformation. 
However, detecting changes within materials with minimal changes in their elastic constants is a significant challenge for these methods.
Fortunately, a novel combination of digital image correlation techniques and finite element modeling allows us to analyze the interior deformation of materials even when their elastic properties don't change noticeably.
In this research, we have developed a method to study the deformation of materials with complex structures, and have successfully tested it using two materials: one made of glass and the other made of a rubber-like material.
By utilizing this method, we have discovered that the deformation of materials with irregular structures can be unpredictable and lead to fracture even before failure, and have discovered a correlation between the deformation of these materials and the stress within them.
Moreover, we have found that materials with predictable deformation structures are less prone to unpredictable deformation and that changing their shape can make them more resistant to such deformation. 
These findings have significant implications for our understanding of how materials deform and fail, and could lead to new ways of preventing material failure. 
For example, we have found that applying stress in a specific direction can prevent the material from collapsing and that shaping the material in a specific way can also have this effect.
Ultimately, we have found that controlling a material's microstructure can prevent unpredictable deformation and that this knowledge could be used to develop new materials that are resistant to such deformation.

We also discuss the occurrence of limit cycles in the $\beta$-function of the 2d Gross-Neveu model and the QCD $\beta$-function in the presence of instantons.  In addition, we discuss the general principles that govern the occurrence of limit cycles in quantum field theory models and the emergence of non-trivial fixed points in the renormalization group flow. A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for certain graph classes using the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation for maximum CSPs with constraints defined by arbitrary non-negative functions.

This research is extended to CSPs with constraints that have multiple possible values. The only restriction for such constraints is that they contain an element that is at least as acceptable as all other elements.

A new PTAS for general-valued CSPs is achieved, where constraints' acceptability levels are considered. The result indicates that CSPs with arbitrary non-negative values can be distinguished from general-valued CSPs in terms of approximation schemes. Finally, PTAS for CSPs with constraints that have a lowest value and are positive is achieved. The result shows that CSPs with constraints that have a lowest value and are positive can be distinguished from general-valued CSPs in terms of approximation schemes. Nonetheless, employing such networks for critical life-altering decisions demands a deeper understanding of their decision-making processes. Unfortunately, most artificial neural networks, including DNNs, function as opaque systems, hindering insight into their internal workings. Although some research has initiated the quest to illuminate their behavior, the field of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) remains underdeveloped. rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed increases towards its outer regions rather than its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. There are two possible explanations for this internal rotation pattern arrangement: either this star has undergone a specific internal process or external torque that has maintained its current configuration, or its observed rotation rate only reflects a temporary, evolutionary phase-specific condition. Given the star's age, we've modeled its evolution and potential internal mixing patterns, and these simulations indicate that a short-lived internal process could account for the disparity between its core and outer rotation rates. Nonetheless, further investigation is needed to confirm these findings and explore the underlying physics.

Unfortunately, accurately predicting the duration a program may run, or even whether it will stop, is generally infeasible.
As a result, modern analysis tools typically focus on specific operations and rely on several simplifying assumptions.
Precisely identifying these constraints and critical program regions generally necessitates access to source code, specialized tools, and domain expertise.
Modifying even a single instruction often forces a repeat of this complex process, which becomes extremely time-consuming during iterative code development for performance-critical software.
We introduce MCAD, a new lightweight framework for analyzing the effects of code modifications at the microarchitectural level in binary programs, providing fast and accurate estimates of throughput changes.
MCAD employs a combination of whole-program emulation and instruction-level analysis to identify critical execution paths and provides a detailed understanding of pipeline events.
This comprehensive information enables accurate prediction of throughput changes resulting from individual instruction modifications.
To validate MCAD, we verify its predictions against actual throughput measurements in 15,000 programs from the SPEC CPU2000 suite, finding a strong correlation between MCAD's estimates and measured results.
We also demonstrate MCAD's ability to determine the criticality of program instructions and reverse-engineered binary code sections.
Overall, MCAD offers a novel, whole-program approach to microarchitectural analysis that facilitates rapid evaluation of code modifications at the binary level.

The interactions between electrons become significantly more pronounced in this configuration, ultimately resulting in multiple ordered phases that display momentum polarization along with spin-valley order. The momentum polarization observed is a direct consequence of exchange interactions, which cause all carriers to coalesce into a small number of bands produced by the electron bands' trigonal warping. time. Organisms' material arrangements, present-day versions of which are built on past evolutionary achievements, ensure their survival through generations. In this context, information theory is adapted (by Abrahamsson and Kanewischer in Physica D 383:132-143, 2020) to study hereditary processes, developing the concept of temporal heredity as a reliable transmission of information from past to present. This work refines that initial study by introducing a hereditary measure applicable to continuous data patterns, using results to demonstrate the stability of temporal heredity over time as patterns evolve. Additionally, examples illustrate how temporal heredity's underlying structure was designed, allowing its modification through evolution. This research reveals a hereditary pattern requires minimal information and confirms the importance of considering patterns' dynamics, rather than their instantaneous configurations, in understanding hereditary processes. As such, temporal heredity provides a framework for quantifying the long-time persistence of patterns that have been maintained through Earth's history. This persistence is linked to patterns' local complexity and their evolution's regularization effect, which has gone unrecognised until now. As a result, our findings offer new insights into patterns' survival over long periods of time. This research provides a framework for using hereditary measures in the study of patterns' persistence, extending beyond Earth's context to other life forms and patterns yet to be discovered on other planets and in other environments. This research opens a new field of study: the long-term survival of patterns.

Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which includes images representing three categories of weather (rain, snow, and fog), and propose a novel algorithm utilizing super-pixel masks for data augmentation to yield satisfactory results using multiple convolutional neural network architectures. 
Our approach achieves a high accuracy of 0.94 in the binary classification of fog against clear skies, a previously unreleased benchmark in the field. 
The dataset and source code are publicly available for the scientific community. 
This research is supported by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada. 
The RFS dataset and associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/fatemehkarimii/rfs_dataset.

In particular, we investigate the analysis of vast systems, comprising numerous copies of entities creating large populations. Due to the replication of entities within these models, their state spaces exponentially expand, making precise stochastic analysis computationally burdensome or impractical.

We introduce a novel approximate aggregation algorithm applicable to large-scale PEPA models describing large populations of entities. This method incorporates an accurate account of the system's overall behavior, based on a stationary distribution calculated over the model's state space. For a system's given time point and a specific property of interest, the algorithm determines how often this property occurs and how fast the system progresses towards achieving the specified property. This method also allows for identifying the speed at which the system reaches a steady state and validates whether the system has reached equilibrium. The approach involves breaking down the system into smaller parts and calculating their individual frequencies. These frequencies are then combined to approximate the desired property, with the result being expressed as an error margin. The algorithm's time and space complexity are directly proportional to the number of model's active states. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in two case studies. In particular, we analyze a system describing a large population of entities waiting for service and a system simulating the large-scale failure of components in a system. These studies showcase the algorithm's ability to accurately calculate the speeds of events and verify the system's correctness. Moreover,

Developing this specialized hardware efficiently requires an agile and dynamic hardware development approach.  However, there is a notable lack of up-to-date tools capable of supporting such an innovative methodology.  In particular, there is an acute need for more effective tools in both design and verification phases.  In response to this need, the authors of this paper propose a new verification tool called ChiselVerify.  ChiselVerify is an open-source tool for checking the integrity of electronic circuits designed with the help of any hardware design language.  ChiselVerify is built on top of Chisel, utilizing Scala and the Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) for testing and verification purposes.  ChiselVerify is centered around three key concepts.  Firstly, the tool is designed to enhance the productivity of verification engineers by facilitating hardware testing within modern, high-level programming environments.  Secondly, the versatility of Chisel allows the tool to work seamlessly with a wide range of hardware design languages.  Thirdly, the tool is closely integrated with the existing Chisel universe, serving as a complementary extension of current testing libraries.  ChiselVerify's design was inspired by SystemVerilog functionalities, providing verification engineers with a wide range of testing capabilities such as functional coverage, constrained-random verification, bus functional modeling, and more within a high-level programming environment. Our findings indicate that, under specific conditions dependent on the object's spin, the ASTG can generate repulsive gravitational fields in the polar regions of massive objects, thereby shedding new light on the phenomenon of outflows as a manifestation of repulsive gravity. This process is an integral component of star formation and has been the subject of extensive debate regarding its origins. This paper diverges from the conventional understanding of gravitation, presenting it as a force that, in certain contexts, drives material apart rather than pulling it together towards a central point. Furthermore, we present empirical evidence that suggests the Azimuthally Symmetric Gravitational Field derived from the ASTG can effectively resolve a theoretical dilemma surrounding massive star formation known as the Radiation Problem, where the high levels of radiation from the developing star can inhibit further accretion of surrounding material. Our analysis reveals that, contrary to expectations, accretion is not obstructed at great distances from the star, thereby providing a potential explanation for how massive stars are able to form despite obstacles to accretion. Moreover, our theory offers a novel perspective on the role of outflows in star formation, postulating that they may arise from the repulsive gravitational effect of the star's spin on surrounding material, rather than simply being a byproduct of the star's formation as previously understood. The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which we subsequently test through benchmarking analysis.
While Delegated RingCT may not possess the same level of anonymity compared to other RingCT implementations, we propose that its ability to be compatible with DPoS consensus mechanisms provides a reasonable trade-off for enabling a more efficient and scalable decentralized cryptocurrency with maintained anonymity capabilities. 
The test results demonstrate that our solution is viable, and the stored values can be recovered quickly, with computational overheads being acceptable. 
Furthermore, performance optimization, including caching, significantly enhances the efficiency of our protocol, reducing the computational time to nearly instantaneous. 
Subject to the constraints of DPoS, Delegated RingCT offers a more practical solution for achieving anonymous transactions within a decentralized environment. 
We believe that Delegated RingCT can serve as a more feasible consensus mechanism in low-resource settings, such as IoT devices, while also being suitable for user-centric applications where a relatively lower level of anonymity is tolerated. 
In particular, Delegated RingCT has the potential to be adopted in cryptocurrencies targeting user-centric applications or consensus mechanisms for IoT systems

These observations extend the range of boson creation under which the LHC can operate by nearly 300 GeV for pairs of bosons and also provide restrictions on potential theories beyond the standard model where boson creation is involved.  These limitations are seen in several models that attempt to explain phenomena at higher energy levels and also provide restrictions on boson creation at lower energy levels, such as in collisions at 13 TeV with squared energy transfer of 2 TeV.  These discoveries provide further evidence of the accuracy of the standard model at high energy levels and motivate searches for even more complex particles at higher energy levels, such as in collisions at 33 TeV and also provide further restrictions on boson creation

Given the complexity and precision issues associated with calculating higher-order terms, developing various resummation methods has become crucial in minimizing computational costs while producing accurate thermodynamic estimates. A recent breakthrough presented a resummation method to all orders of the chemical potential by incorporating charge density correlation functions into the Taylor series. However, since these correlation functions are calculated stochastically from various random volume sources, biased estimates arise which significantly skew results, especially for large values of the number of correlation functions and the chemical potential. Moreover, at lower temperatures, certain higher-order derivatives of the free energy become distorted. This research proposes a new resummation method built upon a Gaussian approximation that fully incorporates all available correlation functions. In contrast to the standard Taylor series approach, higher-order derivatives are no longer necessary, thereby minimizing computational costs. Our findings demonstrate that this new method accurately estimates thermodynamic quantities at both high and low temperatures, exhibiting substantial cost reductions. While the associated systematic errors emerge from incomplete large volume correction, volume effects can be further minimized through an ongoing technique known as the global fit method. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems. Furthermore, the article introduces a novel concept of linear distance between functions in metric spaces and establishes its significance. Ultimately, the article demonstrates that any space with angle function can be viewed as having a unique set of functions, which it calls Euclidean representations, possessing certain key properties. These representations enable the generalization of various fundamental theorems from Euclidean geometry to the broader context of metric spaces. Interestingly, the article shows that the embedding of spaces with angle function into Euclidean spaces, as desired in Menger's problems, can actually be derived naturally from the Euclidean representations themselves. Moreover, the article presents a generalized version of the theorem that states the image of a circle under a homeomorphism is also a circle. Lastly, the article introduces the concept of circle groups within this new framework and establishes the theorem that the image of a circle under a homeomorphism is indeed another circle,

distributions during the training process. MDN leverages regression analysis,
using a decoder network, to transform metadata into a form that does not

normalization module, MDN prevents features from being biased by metadata.

generalization of downstream tasks and prevents features from being
contaminated by metadata. MDN is compatible with a range of normalizations

Nevertheless, the standard finite element methods that employ the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements tend to have low spatial accuracy in the vector transport equation. This paper explores two methods that elevate the accuracy of transporting such vector-valued fields across curved surfaces in two-dimensional environments. One method enhances the transported field by projecting it onto a higher-order function space before solving the transport equation. In contrast, the other method utilizes a mixed finite element approach to concurrently solve for both the transported field and its vorticity, introducing a stabilisation strategy via a Streamline Upwind Petrov-Galerkin method. deep learning techniques can quickly establish models without the need for thorough system knowledge, similar to physics-based modeling approaches. Nevertheless, this simplified modeling comes with a cost: the need to verify the model's trustworthiness due to concerns about its reliability. This research introduces an innovative method, incorporating physics into adversarial machine learning (ML), which aims to increase the confidence that the model adheres to physical principles. The proposed method first identifies the model's limitations through an adversarial testing phase, searching for inputs that highlight discrepancies between the model's behavior and real-world operational scenarios. Next, the model undergoes adversarial training informed by physics, allowing it to learn from its mistakes through an iterative process that corrects errors in counterexamples. The efficacy of this adversarial ML approach was demonstrated in a practical evaluation involving two aircraft system performance models, successfully detecting inconsistencies in both models and improving their alignment with physical principles. Moreover, this research shows that the model can be adversarially trained for up to 20 epochs without suffering from the performance degradation often associated with such training methods. The findings of this research underscore the potential of this novel approach for assessing the reliability of ML models in engineering and scientific applications. considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions regarding the implications of these negations and performed a series of challenging tasks: paraphrasing negated statements, altering the scope of negation, and reversing the negation, resulting in distinct groups of question-answer pairs that current models struggle to tackle without resorting to workarounds. Our CONDAQA dataset comprises 14,182 challenging question-answer pairs, encompassing over 200 unique negation cues and proves particularly demanding for leading NLP models. Notably, even the best-performing model (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) managed only 42% accuracy according to our consistency metric, significantly lagging behind the 81% achieved by human evaluators. In a bid to fuel further NLP innovation, we publicly release our dataset, along with comprehensive evaluations involving fully-finetuned, few-shot, and zero-shot scenarios. Our research aims to stimulate the development of NLP models that better incorporate negation, ultimately enabling them to outperform human evaluators in generating accurate implications from negated statements. Nevertheless, the volatility of system state remains a concern, as this affects the program's ability to access and execute from a crash point. In this research, we investigate the practical limits of developing an instant snapshot algorithm that creates a stable memory environment by freezing all volatile states at the moment of a crash. Our key contribution is the creation of a simple, general algorithm that accomplishes this and is further enhanced by an optimized version offering significantly reduced pause time. We demonstrate through experimental results that the optimized version yields a less than one percent slowdown in average pause time compared to a pure checkpointing approach. Additionally, our results show that the cost of taking a snapshot is directly proportional to the volume of data written during program execution. We believe that our findings offer a viable solution for instant snapshot problems. As an extension of our work, we develop a linear-time algorithm to determine the start and end points of a program's execution segments, thereby enabling an optimized snapshot process that minimizes pause time. We also introduce and validate two new benchmarks, namely sort-tree and push-pair, specifically designed to test the robustness of instant snapshot algorithms. Our experiments reveal that these benchmarks pose more challenging conditions for instant snapshots compared to traditional benchmarks like matrix multiplication and page turn. opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum many-body system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phase of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modification and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship enables the identification of the annealing gap's critical points even in cases where equilibrium simulations are impractical due to limitations in computing power. We illustrate the effectiveness of this approach in a complex optimization problem derived from a chemical reaction simulation. This study provides a crucial link between quantum annealing and quenching, offering a novel observational tool for analyzing quantum many-body systems that cannot be solved through current classical methods. This research also opens up a new avenue of research: using quench patterns to control the annealing gap and devise more efficient quantum annealing protocols. Furthermore, the techniques described here can be applied to other types of dynamical scenarios, such as quantum critical quenching, which can lead to the transfer of information across systems. Finally, the methods discussed can be adapted for detecting topological properties in systems and for creating topological states through dynamical quenches.

Data indicates that nearly 88% of defendants with mental health disorders do not receive support unless their attorneys notify the court.  An analysis also shows that defendants who receive bail are more likely to receive a mental health diagnosis.  Importantly, the research highlights disparities in how defendants with mental health disorders are treated, including prolonged cases, increased likelihood of bail, and heightened risks of additional charges, particularly among female defendants and those with schizophrenia or bipolar disorder.  Ultimately, these findings suggest a mental health disorder may act as an unseen obstacle for defendants in navigating the criminal justice system, as evident from the observed disparities.  To address these disparities, the study recommends implementing procedures that encourage more frequent notifications from defense attorneys and providing training on mental health disorders

We argue this two-part approach has limitations in understanding the evidence provided by the p-value. As an alternative, we propose replacing it with the probability of the test, a concept introduced by Deborah Mayo that encompasses both the null and alternative hypotheses. By adopting this probability of the test, we believe researchers can gain more insight into the results, avoid unnecessary decisions, and encourage further investigation. Furthermore, we show that the probability of the test can be broken down into components that separately evaluate the null and alternative hypotheses. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in a simulation study and also illustrate its application in two real-world experiments. Through this exploration, we aim to promote a more informed use of the p-value that acknowledges its connection to the probability of the test, thereby encouraging a more in-depth examination of the results. Our goal is to contribute to a shift in the way researchers think about the p-value, ultimately aiming for a testing paradigm that is more aligned with Mayo's'severe testing' philosophy. By embracing this perspective, we can collectively uncover subpar models and theories, even when the evidence against them is short of being definitive. In effect, we believe that the probability of the test can serve as a nuanced indicator of the reliability of tests, especially when evaluated over the long term. As a result, we recommend prioritizing the probability of the test as a primary consideration in testing decisions,

The novel architecture combines the strengths of Residual-Recursive Networks and supplementary regularization techniques to efficiently derive 3D shape and camera parameters from 2D keypoints data. To address the problem's inherent under-determination, PR-RRN is augmented with two novel pairwise regularization terms. Under certain data transformations and assuming normal distribution of a dataset, a t-statistic provides a precise p-value. The presence of non-linear relationships, however, complicates p-value calculation. This study investigates how differential data transformations impact the results of a t-test used to assess correlation. Specifically, we analyze how various common transformations, such as the log, square root, and Box-Cox methods, influence the output of a t-test and the consistency of p-value calculations. Our research highlights that each transformation has unique properties and selecting an appropriate method is crucial to produce consistent results. The log transformation is found to be reliable in cases where data exhibits a wide range of positive values, whereas the square root transformation performs well with data characterized by a small standard deviation. The Box-Cox transformation emerges as a robust option for diverse datasets with varying levels of non-normality. Our research strongly suggests that simply using a single, universal transformation will not produce reliable results and that each data set should be evaluated individually to determine the most suitable transformation. The study also emphasizes the importance of using a data-driven approach to select the most appropriate transformation. The research reveals that using such transformations can significantly improve the accuracy and consistency of p-value calculations for a t-test. Additionally, our investigation demonstrates that these transformations have a profound impact on power, particularly in cases where data is not normally distributed

Despite superior accuracy when large datasets are available, Deep Neural Networks struggle when data are scarce, which hampers practical applications. One key benefit of combining physics rules with machine learning techniques is that trained models can produce accurate results using less available data, as they're based on physically logical premises. In a paper, the feasibility of incorporating monotonic constraints in a Gaussian Process (GP) framework was investigated for data from three materials, utilizing one real-world and two computer-generated datasets. These findings were initially reported in the paper 'Universal scaling for defect diffusion' published in Nature Communications in 2019. It was suggested in the paper that a specific relationship exists between the diffusion coefficient and the binding energy of defects, which applies universally across all materials. However, this conclusion hinges on the incorrect assumption that the diffusion coefficient is solely determined by the defect's hopping frequency. In reality, the diffusion coefficient is a composite value that also takes into account the defect's jump probability and the time between jumps. In the case of the carbon vacancy in silicon, the jump probability is significantly lower than what was reported in the paper, resulting in a diffusion coefficient that is also much lower. As such, the predictions based on the universal scaling law are no longer valid. In particular, the activation energy for diffusion that was reported in the paper does not apply to the carbon vacancy in silicon and should be disregarded. In fact, the diffusion of carbon vacancies in silicon is much faster than what was claimed in the paper. In the case of the silicon self-interstitial, the picture is more complicated as the diffusion coefficient is also influenced by the presence of multiple possible structural forms, each with its own hopping frequency and jump probability. Knowledge graph embeddings (KGE) is a popular method to tackle this problem, which converts entities and relationships into low-dimensional vectors to predict unobserved relationships. However, this approach only employs basic logic to encode available triplets, but struggles to apply universal rules (for example, "all x's wife is x's husband"). Traditional rule-based KG reasoning systems, on the other hand, often depend on rigid rule inference and can be brittle. We introduce RulE, a novel framework that represents and models both logical rules and triplets within a single unified space. This research aims to explore the factors that contribute to the emergence and sustainability of cooperative patterns by dynamically varying the prisoner's dilemma game's payoff matrix. These capabilities enable the system to provide a suggested initial route, update the route in real-time as the user moves, and recommend timely corrections to their path. Our experimental results demonstrate the system's accuracy in navigating unfamiliar environments, both indoors and outdoors, with an error margin of less than 0.5 meters. Notably, the system is solely reliant on a low-cost, wearable camera, making it a cost-effective solution. Our research findings indicate that the system's suggested initial route is accurate 70% of the time, and within one meter of the final destination 90% of the time. Moreover, the system's ability to adapt to obstacles and suggest corrections to the user's path proves to be a crucial component, especially when navigating complex, dynamic environments. To address the underdetermined problem of calculating the depth map in a geometrically and temporally consistent manner, we aim for plausible and continuous depth estimates in a scene. This study investigates the issue of inferring constraints from observational data of an agent's compliant behavior. Experimental validation is performed to verify that the proposed method successfully identifies the most relevant constraints an agent is expected to follow. Resource Allocation (ONRA) plays a vital role in service provisioning. As a sequential problem with uncertain outcomes, it presents a suitable case for tackling via Reinforcement Learning (RL). However, current RL solutions face significant challenges stemming from high sample complexity requirements. To navigate this hurdle, training RL agents in isolation is impractical due to a lack of knowledge about future service demands, while online training in actual networks causes performance deterioration due to temporary sub-optimal policies during prolonged learning periods. This degradation is particularly pronounced in non-stationary ONRA scenarios, where adapting to shifting service requirements is crucial. To circumvent this problem, a model-based resource allocation framework called RADAR is proposed, designed for ONRA applications with immediately known action rewards. By strategically balancing exploration of the state space in the background with real-time policy exploitation, leveraging synthetic data generated from the trained environment model, RADAR effectively boosts sample efficiency. When applied to a multi-domain service federation problem to maximize profits by selecting suitable domains for service request placement, RADAR showcases its ability to adapt continuously and achieves notable performance gains, specifically up to a 44% improvement over standard RL models without prior knowledge. Moreover, the empirical evaluations demonstrate that RADAR achieves compelling results even in comparison to an all-knowing policy optimizer. To validate the practical applicability and autonomy of RADAR, a multi-domain service federation scenario with dynamically changing service demands and domain characteristics is employed, allowing RADAR to continuously adapt and maintain optimal performance. In this paper, we propose an efficient and straightforward high-order method for calculating Newtonian potentials based on Green's identity, which simplifies the complex volume integration into boundary integrals. These boundary integrals can then be computed quickly using the Helsing-Ojala method. Our new method makes expensive computations of near field interactions feasible on a grid-free basis, enabling us to study the detailed structures of Newtonian potentials thoroughly. In the case of a point mass, we derive an explicit formula for the potential within any closed bounded area. Furthermore, we show that applying Green's first identity allows us to express the potential at any point as the sum of a "far-field" term (the logarithmic term) and a "near-field" term, which involves integrating the mass function over a small area around the observation point. Using this near-field term, we are able to obtain highly accurate approximations of the potential at close proximity to the mass. In the case of multiple point masses, we also obtain explicit formulas for the potential at any point and a highly accurate near-field term.
